paper_title: UniVEP: Unifying Velocity and Endpoint Prediction for Robot Manipulation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Flow-matching robot policies usually use one prediction target throughout action generation, even though recovering actions from noise and polishing nearly clean actions bring different challenges. We systematically compare velocity prediction (V), endpoint prediction (X), and velocity-weighted endpoint prediction (X--V) across multiple robot policies, benchmarks, and inference budgets. On StarVLA and LiLa-WAM, X--V works best for few-step generation, while V gains more from iterative refinement. We further uncover their complementary strengths across noise levels: clean actions have concentrated covariance spectra, endpoint predictions stay more stable under high noise, and velocity predictions offer more accurate corrections near clean actions. Inspired by these findings, we introduce UniVEP, which learns both prediction targets together with consistency supervision and switches from endpoint recovery to velocity refinement as noise drops. Each step only needs one network run, and joint training also boosts single-step endpoint generation. Tests on simulated and real-world manipulation show better success rates and efficiency. On RoboTwin, UniVEP hits 61.36% success with one StarVLA run, beating the best single-target baseline at sixteen runs (59.96%). With LiLa-WAM, two runs outperform the best sixteen-step single-target baseline and cut inference latency by 77.1%.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Generative robot policies can produce rich, continuous action sequences, but they must do so quickly enough for closed-loop control. Modern vision-language-action (VLA) policies and world-action models (WAMs) commonly use flow matching to transform Gaussian noise into executable action chunks [2, 33, 47, 50]. Each refinement step requires another network evaluation, creating trade-off between action quality and control latency. While much effort has gone into reducing sampling steps [37, 45, 53], we revisit more basic question: what should the action network predict? Most flow-based policies predict the velocity that transports noisy action toward the data. An alternative is to predict the clean action endpoint directly. Although these two predictions are analytically interchangeable along linear noise-to-data path [1, 25, 29], they pose different learning problems. Endpoint prediction seeks structured action, whereas velocity prediction must also account for the injected noise. Moreover, generation itself changes character over time: the model first needs to recover an action from heavy noise, then make increasingly precise corrections as the sample approaches valid trajectory. There is little reason to expect one prediction target to be equally effective at both stages, from early recovery to final refinement. We investigate this question by comparing three objectives: velocity prediction (V), direct endpoint prediction (X), and endpoint prediction with velocity-weighted loss (XV), as explored in actionmanifold learning [46, 48]. Our study covers three policy architecturesStarVLA, FastWAM, and LiLa-WAM [44, 47, 50]on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin 2.0 [5, 10, 26]. Within each policy, we keep the architecture, training data, and update budget fixed while varying inference from one to sixteen network evaluations. On StarVLA and LiLa-WAM, XV performs particularly well with one or two evaluations, while benefits substantially from additional steps. Direct X, in contrast, improves little as the budget grows. The best prediction objective therefore depends not only on the policy, but also on how many refinement steps it can afford. Why does this ranking change? We examine the structure of the targets and the behavior of their predictions along the noise-to-action path. Clean action chunks have far more concentrated sample covariance spectra than velocity targets or Gaussian noise. At high noise, endpoint predictions remain substantially more stable across different noise initializations. Near clean action, velocity-based updates produce lower recovery error: they correct the current estimate rather than predicting the entire action again. These results point to natural division of labor (Figure 1): endpoint prediction for recovering actions from noise, and velocity prediction for refining them near the end of generation. Guided by this finding, we introduce UniVEP (Unifying Velocity and Endpoint Prediction). UniVEP trains both prediction modes within shared action network, using consistency objective to align the clean actions implied by each mode. velocity-weighted endpoint loss further strengthens endpoint supervision. During sampling, UniVEP first predicts endpoints at high noise and then switches to velocity prediction for low-noise refinement. Each step evaluates only the selected mode, retaining the inference cost of single-target policy. Joint training also strengthens the endpoint predictor, allowing the policy to generate effective action chunks with single network evaluation. The resulting gains extend across simulated and real-robot manipulation. On RoboTwin Clean, UniVEP with StarVLA achieves 61.36% success in one evaluation, exceeding the strongest single-target baseline at sixteen evaluations (59.96%). On LiLa-WAM, two evaluations achieve 85.96% success, surpassing the best sixteen-step single-target result (82.60%) while cutting action-generation latency by 77.1%. On three real dual-arm tasks, mean success increases from 49.33% to 58.67%. Our contributions are threefold: 1. Comprehensive comparison of prediction targets. We systematically study V, X, and XV across multiple VLA and WAM architectures, manipulation benchmarks, and inference budgets, revealing distinct performance trends as the sampling-step budget changes. 2 2. Understanding their complementary strengths. Through action-space statistics and noise-conditioned prediction probes, we find that endpoint prediction is more stable at high noise, whereas velocity prediction is more effective for near-clean refinement. 3. UniVEP for efficient robot manipulation. We unify endpoint and velocity prediction through joint supervision and noise-dependent switching. Across the policies we evaluate, UniVEP achieves strong manipulation performance with one or two network evaluations. At the same number of sampling steps, it matches the inference FLOPs of single-target policy.

sections.title: 2.1 Prediction targets in generative models
sections.content: Diffusion and flow models predict noise, velocity, or clean data. Although algebraically related, these targets impose different learning objectives on finite networks [12, 16, 1820, 25, 31]. Recent studies connect target selection to data structure: JiT favors clean-image prediction [23], AsymFlow uses full-rank data and low-rank noise [4], and MFlow blends targets along principal directions [32]. The influence of data dimensionality has also been investigated [17]. SC-Flow is the closest methodological precedent [14]. It jointly predicts velocity and endpoints within shared network, enforces consistency between them, and switches from endpoint to velocity updates during sampling. Building on this formulation, UniVEP investigates observation-conditioned robot actions, where prediction quality must translate into closed-loop task success. We systematically examine prediction objectives across inference budgets and noise levels, together with velocity-weighted supervision and its interaction with pretrained action heads.

sections.title: 2.2 Prediction objectives for robot actions
sections.content: Diffusion policies generate action chunks via iterative denoising [6, 27, 34, 38, 52], while flow-based policies learn velocity fields [2, 3, 33, 36, 41]. World-action models further couple actions with future visual features or video [28, 40, 43, 47, 49, 50, 54]. For dexterous video prediction, DexAC-WM [51] preserves dimension-level action structure through per-dimension tokenization. Alternatively, ABot-M0 and multi-view Action Manifold Learning predict clean actions under velocity-space supervision [46, 48], matching our XV baseline except its bounded weighting. MM-ABC also reports gains from clean-action prediction [24]. We distinguish prediction targets from their training losses by comparing V, X, and XV under matched training setups on StarVLA, FastWAM, and LiLa-WAM [44, 47, 50]. Evaluations on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin [5, 10, 26] cover different inference budgets, perturbations, and scene randomization. We further investigate how velocity-oriented pretraining influences target selection in world-action models tied to video backbone.

sections.title: 2.3 Few-step generative control
sections.content: Consistency Policy, ManiCM, and FlowPolicy accelerate robot action generation through consistency learning or distillation [13, 37, 53]. One-Step Diffusion Policy and One-Step Flow Policy pursue single-evaluation control [22, 45]. Much Ado About Noising analyzes intermediate supervision, stochasticity, and iterative computation in generative robot control [35]. Rather than distilling separate student, we study prediction objectives within existing policies, distinguishing gains from joint training at one or two evaluations from those due to endpoint-to-velocity switching at larger budgets on both StarVLA and LiLa-WAM.

sections.title: 4 Analyzing Prediction Targets
sections.content: The target structure in Section 3.3 motivates comparison of V, X, and XV in closed-loop control. We first measure task success across inference budgets, then probe how the learned predictions behave at different noise levels. These observations guide the design of UniVEP in Section 5.

sections.title: 5 UniVEP
sections.content: The findings in Section 4.3 suggest different roles for endpoint and velocity prediction during action generation. UniVEP brings both modes into single action policy: training supervises both predictions, while inference evaluates only the mode selected for the current noise level (Figure 4).

sections.title: 6.5 Inference Efficiency
sections.content: Finding 13: UniVEP achieves strong control with unchanged counted FLOPs and comparable latency at matched inference budgets. At matched policy and NFE, UniVEP evaluates one prediction mode per step and has the same counted inference FLOPs as the single-target recipes. At the native budgets, the cost per action chunk is 2.411 TFLOPs for StarVLA (4 NFE), 0.466 for LiLa-WAM (10 NFE), and 4.041 for FastWAM (10 NFE). At the native budgets in Table 7, each UniVEP variants measured latency stays within approximately 3% of that of the corresponding single-target recipes. Reducing the number of evaluations yields larger savings. One-step StarVLA UniVEP (61.36%, 61.59 ms) exceeds 16-step XV (59.96%, 191.32 ms), 67.8% latency reduction. Two-step LiLa-WAM UniVEP (85.96%, 23.16 ms) exceeds the 10-step XV baseline (83.48%, 67.75 ms) at 65.8% lower latency; against the 16-step XV baseline (82.60%, 100.98 ms), the reduction is 77.1%. Joint training has separate training-time cost: for StarVLA on one A800, it adds 6.93% counted FLOPs and 15.57% per-update time over  (Table 12)  . Timing protocols and additional controls are in Section C.3.

sections.title: 6.6 Real-World Bimanual Manipulation
sections.content: We evaluate UniVEP on 14-DoF ARX A7 dual-arm platform equipped with an egocentric Intel RealSense D405 depth camera. The hardware configuration and workspace are shown in Figure 5(a). The policy takes 224 224 egocentric image, language instruction, and 14-dimensional joint state as input, and predicts 16-step chunks of absolute joint positions. We consider three manipulation tasks that probe sequential object interaction, bimanual coordination, and precise gripper alignment: Table 8. Real-robot success (%). Task Drawer Cube Place Pick Two Cube Grab Stick 24 32 34 34 46 38 34 76 Mean 31.33 38. 49.33 14 XV UniVEP 52 40 84 58. Figure 5. Real-world setup and three dual-arm tasks. (a) ARX A7 platform with RealSense D405 camera. (b) Drawer Cube Place. (c) Pick Two Cube. (d) Grab Stick. Drawer Cube Place: The robot opens drawer and places cube inside, requiring successful execution of successive manipulation stages (Figure 5(b)). Pick Two Cube: The robot grasps two cubes, one with each gripper, and place both on the plate, testing coordinated control of both arms (Figure 5(c)). Grab Stick: The robot grasps slender rod, testing the precision of gripper positioning and alignment (Figure 5(d)). We collect 50 demonstrations per task and train one multitask StarVLA policy for each prediction recipe: V, X, XV, and UniVEP. All policies use the same demonstrations and are trained for 20,000 updates with batch size of 32. We evaluate each policy for 50 trials per task and report the success rate. All policies generate each action chunk using four Euler integration steps, corresponding to four calls. We retain the original StarVLA controller across all recipes, keeping the inference budget and action interface matched. As shown in Table 8, UniVEP achieves 58.67% mean success, outperforming the strongest single-target baseline, XV, by 9.3 percentage points. Gains are consistent across all three tasks: Drawer Cube Place improves from 38% to 52%, Grab Stick from 76% to 84%, and Pick Two Cube from 34% to 40%. The largest gain on Drawer Cube Place demonstrates benefits for successive object interactions. Qualitatively, UniVEP produces smoother arm motions with fewer abrupt corrections during reaching and grasping, consistent with velocity-based refinement near the clean-action endpoint.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: We revisited the prediction objective of flow-based robot policies through controlled comparisons across architectures, benchmarks, and inference budgets. On StarVLA and LiLa-WAM, velocity-weighted endpoint prediction is particularly effective with few evaluations, while velocity prediction benefits more from iterative refinement. Noise-conditioned probes show complementary behavior: endpoint estimates are less sensitive to noise initialization, whereas velocity predictions produce more accurate near-clean corrections. UniVEP combines these modes in shared, consistently supervised policy. Joint training strengthens endpoint prediction even when inference uses only one or two evaluations; at larger budgets, endpoint-to-velocity switching adds refinement without increasing per-step inference FLOPs. The result is stronger few-step manipulation and lower generation latency, with additional gains on three real bimanual tasks. FastWAMs velocity-pretrained action head remains notable exception, showing that changing the prediction objective can depend strongly on initialization. Learning the switching rule from policy-specific evidence, rather than fixing it globally, is promising direction for future work.
